items.item: S3's cost is split across six distinct components: storage, request/retrieval, transfer, data-management, replication, and transform/query.

at.step: Reveal: five cost classes, priced per unit of business

items.item: Storage itself is priced by the combination of object size, duration stored, and storage class.

items.item: A bill is usually dominated by one term, and optimizing the others first is wasted effort.

items.item: Scan volume, cross-AZ traffic, and idle compute are the three shapes a dominating bar usually takes, and naming the shape is the real diagnostic step.
A lever's saving is a measured ratio against the actual bill, not a guess.

at.step: Reveal: a lever, and its measured ratio

items.item: The lever that fixes one dominator does nothing for a different one — it's specific to the dominator, not a generic optimization.
Every lever that lowers one cost has a second-order cost of its own, which must be priced alongside the saving.

at.step: Reveal: every lever has a second-order cost

items.item: A steep enough price change to one cost class can shift which class dominates, so the waterfall is re-run on fresh prices, not assumed to hold.

at.step: Prove it: a new price sheet, the same waterfall

items.item: This topic leaves out FinOps practice, cloud pricing models, infrastructure as code, layout/pruning mechanics, and autoscaling mechanics deliberately — it teaches the design response, not the provider billing mechanics.
Cost-per-unit pricing and waterfall analysis are established FinOps practice, not an emerging technique.

This topic gives the shop a priced design with one dominating lever identified, which the next topic (trade-off articulation and decision records) assumes already exists before putting it in front of someone to defend.
Effort spent tuning a cost class is not evidence that class is the one dominating the bill — the two are checked separately, by running the waterfall rather than by where the team's time went.
